elements.quote: Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the review as an integrative review, consistent with being a systematic review-type report.

elements.quote: Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: A clear main objective is stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: Included studies were not restricted by research design; and had to evaluate the sustainability of an EBI in a healthcare context.
elements.reason: The abstract provides inclusion criteria elements (not restricted by design; must evaluate sustainability in a healthcare context) but does not explicitly specify exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: a comprehensive search strategy was applied across five databases.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies that databases were searched, but it does not specify the information sources with the explicit 'last searched' timing.

elements.quote: We assessed the methodological quality of studies using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess risk/methodological quality of included studies (MMAT).

elements.quote: Methods: Following Whittemore and Knafl's methodological process: (1) problem identification; (2) literature search; (3) data evaluation; (4) data analysis; and (5) presentation, a comprehensive search strategy was applied across five databases.
elements.reason: The abstract outlines the review methods (data evaluation, data analysis, presentation) consistent with how results are synthesized/presented.

elements.quote: Results: Of 18,783 articles retrieved, 64 fit the inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (64) and some characteristics (e.g., qualitative designs most commonly used; common approaches), but does not report total number of participants.

elements.quote: Qualitative designs were most commonly used for evaluation (48%)... Timing of data collection varied widely with post-intervention data collection most frequent (89%). Of the 64 studies, 44% used a framework... Most studies (77%) did not measure sustainability outcomes, rather these studies focused on sustainability determinants.
elements.reason: The abstract provides results relevant to outcomes/approaches (e.g., whether sustainability outcomes were measured; percentages of frameworks/models), but it does not present outcome results for each main outcome with study/participant counts.
No meta-analysis is described in the retrieved abstract evidence, so summary estimate and confidence/credible intervals are not applicable.
The retrieved abstract evidence does not report comparisons between groups or directions of effect; therefore this requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: Discussion: It is unclear which approach/approaches are most effective for evaluating sustainability and what measures and outcomes are most commonly used. There is a disconnect between evaluating the factors that may shape sustainability and the outcomes approaches employed to measure sustainability.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes limitations/uncertainties about effectiveness and the mismatch between determinants and measured outcomes.

elements.quote: Our review offers methodological recommendations for sustainability evaluation research and highlights the importance in understanding mechanisms of sustainability to advance the field.
elements.reason: A general interpretation and implications for future research are provided.
No primary funding source for the review is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No register name and registration number are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Background: There is limited evidence to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) for healthcare improvement... Discussion: It is unclear which approach/approaches are most effective for evaluating sustainability and what measures and outcomes are most commonly used.
elements.reason: The review describes the current state of knowledge (limited evidence) and important uncertainty (unclear which approaches are most effective and which measures/outcomes are most common).

elements.quote: Background: There is limited evidence to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) for healthcare improvement. Through an integrative review, we aimed to identify approaches to evaluate the sustainability of evidence-based interventions (EBIs) and sustainability outcomes.
elements.reason: The importance/need is explained as stemming from limited evidence and the review’s aim to identify approaches for evaluating sustainability.

No explicit statement is provided explaining the need for this review in relation to existing similar systematic reviews (e.g., identifying a prior review and framing this work as an update/replication).
The provided evidence indicates the review focuses on identifying approaches to evaluate sustainability, not on describing a proposed mechanism of action of an intervention effect.

No logic model (hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes) is described in the retrieved evidence, and the review’s rationale presented focuses on evaluation approaches for sustainability rather than constructing a logic model for intervention components/outcomes.

elements.quote: The aim of this integrative review was to identify and synthesize approaches that have been used to evaluate the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare.
elements.reason: The review’s objective/aim is explicitly stated. However, the objective is not presented as a question using a relevant question-formulation framework (only an aim statement is provided).

elements.quote: The aim of this integrative review was to identify and synthesize approaches that have been used to evaluate the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare.
elements.reason: This review aims to identify and synthesize evaluation approaches for sustainability, not to assess intervention effects with planned comparisons; therefore PICO (or an appropriate variant) is not applicable based on the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Articles were included if they: • Were published in a peer-review journal • Were primary research • Had explicit research design and data collection methods • Had an explicit theoretical ­ approach a for sustainability • Were within a healthcare ­ setting • Evaluated the sustainability of an EBI
elements.reason: Eligibility characteristics for study design/data collection methods, theoretical approach, healthcare setting, and evaluating sustainability are specified, but the evidence provided does not clearly specify any follow-up requirements or all relevant question-framework components.

elements.quote: We only included published studies in the English language and peer-reviewed primary studies in this review. ... all gray literature was excluded.
elements.reason: Language (English) and publication/report status (published studies; peer-reviewed primary studies; gray literature excluded) are specified, but the evidence provided does not clearly specify dissemination year criteria.
No evidence is provided describing that the review distinguished exclusion due to outcomes not being measured versus exclusion due to outcome results not being reported.
No evidence is provided specifying groups used in each synthesis or linking those groups to comparisons/objectives.

Although inclusion/exclusion restrictions are mentioned (e.g., independent sustainability evaluation component; exclusion of gray literature/secondary research), no rationale for notable eligibility restrictions is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: We extracted whether an included study evaluated (a) sustainability determinants and (b) sustainability outcomes and how they measured these variables. We defined sustainability determinants as correlates and predictors of sustainability (organizational, contextual, and strategies) and sustainability outcomes as the subsequent impact (healthcare improvement or public health outcomes) of sustained intervention use [5]. To further unpack sustainability outcomes, we extracted and synthesized nine sustainability outcomes across the 64 included studies (Table 3) [6, 15, 16].
elements.reason: The review states what sustainability determinants and sustainability outcomes are and that nine sustainability outcomes were extracted, but the evidence does not clearly present a complete, explicitly enumerated set of all outcome domains “for which data were sought” with defined outcome-domain boundaries/definitions.

elements.quote: Of 64 included studies, 66% ( n = 43) [20, 22, 24, 25, 28, 31, 34, 35, 39-42, 44, 45, 48-59, 63, 65-76, 79-82] had a clear timing for evaluation and 33% ( n = 21) [19, 21, 23, 26, 27, 29, 30, 32, 33, 36-38, 43, 46, 47, 60-62, 64, 77, 78] had unclear timing. Of the 43 studies with clear timing, 42% ( n = 18) evaluated sustainability at a single time point... The remaining 57% ( n = 25) evaluated sustainability at multiple time points...
elements.reason: The review reports timing categories (single vs multiple time points) and notes that evaluation timing/data collection time points are provided in Table 9, but the evidence does not specify the time frame of measurement separately for each outcome domain.
The evidence does not state whether all compatible results within each outcome domain were sought.

elements.quote: Our synthesis indicated that there is a breadth of theoretical approaches and constructs that were considered for the evaluation of the sustainability of EBIs in healthcare that were consistent with other recent synthesis work [6-10]. A recent scoping review and theory analysis [8] found 37 sustainability determinant factors, which grouped into seven themes: (1) characteristics of the innovation / EBP; (2) adopter/user factors influencing sustained use (3) leadership and management influences/factors; (4) inner context (practice setting/organization) factors where EBPs are delivered; (5) inner processes / infrastructure factors that support the EBPs (e.g., processes, methods, systems, structures, or strategies); (6) outer context or broader system factors; and (7) outcomes descriptions without defined factors. These themes are similar to the work of Lennox et al. Most sustainability evaluations included in this study used qualitative research designs (48%), with interviews as the most common data collection method. This finding is consistent with the work of Lennox [6] who reported 59% of their included studies used qualitative methods.
